definition: Abdicate means to formally give up a throne or supreme power, or to abandon a solemn duty.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word abdicate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know abdicate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: When the scandal broke, the young king chose to abdicate rather than drag the crown through the courts, and the throne passed to his cousin by nightfall.
Anyone can resign — a lifeguard, a treasurer, a prime minister; abdicate raises the stakes to sovereign power, the surrender of a crown rather than a job.

Renounce goes further than abdicate: an abdicating king gives up the crown he wears today, while renouncing the throne rejects even the claim to it — for himself and often for his heirs — leaving nothing to return to.

To relinquish is to let go of something you hold — a grip, a claim, control of a project — at any scale, and often reluctantly. Abdicate is narrower and grander: it names the formal surrender of a throne or supreme power. You can relinquish the TV remote; only sovereigns abdicate.

To cede is to hand something over to a specific someone else — territory to a neighbor, power to a rival — usually under pressure or by agreement. Abdicate looks at the giving-up itself: a monarch can abdicate without ceding to anyone in particular, simply laying the crown down.

Abdicate is sharper than 'quit' or 'step down' because it names the formal surrender of sovereign power itself: a cashier quits and a coach steps down, but only someone holding a throne — or an authority nearly as supreme — can abdicate it.
Abdicate is the formal word for surrendering supreme power, above all a throne; it also stretches to duties solemn enough to feel sovereign, as in abdicating one's responsibility.
For ordinary jobs and offices, resign or step down is the right register, and renounce is the word when someone gives up a claim or belief rather than a seat of power.

Queen Marguerite had ruled the island kingdom for fifty-one years when she summoned the council at midsummer.
The harvests were good, the treasury full, her popularity untouched; that, she said, was exactly the point.

She announced that she would abdicate on the equinox, while the choice was still hers -- 'a crown should be set down in calm weather, not pried loose in a storm.' Her ministers protested that no ruler of her line had ever stepped away from power by choice.
She signed the instrument anyway, watched her son crowned by winter, and spent her last years annotating the palace archives as plain Madame Marguerite.
